crime.value: Ambiguous supernatural death(s): Forrest Blake dies suddenly the night he confronts his wife with proof of her adultery, and Janet later drowns in her own pool lured by his apparition. Central question: is Janet being haunted/killed by Forrest's returning spirit, or destroyed by her own guilt?
crime.quote: That is where they found her, face down at the bottom of the quiet pool.

victim.value: Janet Blake, the unfaithful, mercenary younger widow whose adultery and greed were exposed by her husband the night before he died; also Forrest Blake, the elderly, meek husband destroyed by discovering her betrayal
victim.quote: It was the next morning she found him dead.

closed_world.value: The Blake house high in the Burlingame hills — study, bedroom, terrace and pool — plus Janet's tight social circle (Mavis, Olivia, Annie the maid)
closed_world.quote: It was Annie’s day off and she was alone in the big house.

culprit_and_motive.value: Implied culprit is Forrest's returning ghost (the white moth/lost soul), avenging his humiliation and betrayal by drawing Janet into the pool; alternatively Janet's own guilt and drinking
culprit_and_motive.quote: she saw Forrest catch it and hold it out to her... following him as he beckoned her on to the middle of the pool

resolution.value: No investigative resolution; closure is supernatural — Janet drowns clutching a white moth that revives and flies away, suggesting a soul released
resolution.quote: she gently pried open a fist clenched around a bedraggled white moth, then screamed hysterically as it... lurched crazily away

investigator.value: No detective; the lens is Janet herself — guilty widow and eventual victim, whose recollections reveal the secret
investigator.quote: Huddled in Forrest’s big chair by the fireplace... Janet reviewed the nightmare of the past weeks.

suspect_architecture.value: No formal suspect cast; the story is a psychological haunting. Potential culpable figures implied around Janet's guilt: Janet herself (adulterous wife with motive to want Forrest dead and inheriting his fortune), the greedy young lover who sold her out, and Forrest himself (possible suicide/resignation to death). Peripheral figures — Annie the superstitious maid, Mavis Carter the sympathetic friend, Olivia Randall, Jack Loren — serve as witnesses rather than suspects.
suspect_architecture.quote: Rotten luck it had to be Forrest who found her out. But Forrest was dead, wasn’t he?

red_herring.value: The apparitions of Forrest are framed as literal supernatural returns (reinforced by Annie's folklore of white moths as lost souls), misdirecting from the reading that they are alcohol-fuelled guilt hallucinations luring Janet to her death.
red_herring.quote: “It’s a poor, lost soul trying to find a resting place. It was Mr. Blake himself...who told me never to kill a white moth

clue_fairness.value: Clues are planted openly for the reader: the baroque apartment key Forrest bought from the lover, Forrest's undisclosed appointment and intent to see his lawyer, his heart-broken resignation on the drive home, Janet's escalating brandy consumption, and the recurring white moth motif — all shown in scene before the drowning.
clue_fairness.quote: Forrest had reached in his pocket and drawn out a heavy, baroque key which he fingered thoughtfully before Janet’s stunned gaze.

social_world.value: Affluent Burlingame hill-country society: a younger trophy wife dependent on an elderly rich husband, charity board memberships as respectable cover, a circle of 'deadliest friends' who feed on each other's scandal, and servants (Annie) bound by loyalty and folk belief. Power rests on money, alimony risk, and social standing.
social_world.quote: just the innermost circle of her deadliest friends, since outwardly she was observing the amenities of mourning

reveal_mechanic.value: The final image demonstrates rather than states: Janet is found drowned with a white moth clenched in her fist, and the moth — pried loose by Annie — revives and flies away, confirming the moth-as-soul motif and that the apparition led her into the pool.
reveal_mechanic.quote: she gently pried open a fist clenched around a bedraggled white moth, then screamed hysterically as it imperceptibly moved its bruised wing

media_and_audience.value: The crime/death is packaged by gossip rather than press: Janet's circle 'rehash the events' and dissect her disintegration with pleasure, while superstition (white moths as wandering souls) supplies the folk narrative explaining Forrest's return.
media_and_audience.quote: taking advantage of her absence to rehash the events as they knew them before and after Forrest’s sudden death

investigator_wound.value: Janet is the de facto investigator of her own haunting; the case exploits her guilt over the discovered affair, her humiliation at being caught, her terror of aging and of losing money, and her drinking — vulnerabilities that turn the apparitions from horror into comfort and finally into lethal lure.
investigator_wound.quote: her anguish was not regret for her philandering, only that she had been caught. It was humiliating; so damned humiliating

victims_enemies.value: Forrest Blake's enemy is his own wife Janet, who resented his age and meekness and had carried on years of affairs; secondarily the greedy young lover who sold her out to Forrest for money, betraying both.
victims_enemies.quote: This, then, was his dirty revenge, to sell her out to her husband.

suspect_wounds.value: Janet's wound is vanity and terror of aging poverty — the fear of divorce without alimony, and her relief at Forrest's death, make her look and feel like a murderer even though no crime is proven.
suspect_wounds.quote: her first reaction was to laugh aloud in sheer relief. “I’ve always been lucky,” she told herself

unreliable_frame.value: The entire story is filtered through Janet's guilt-saturated, brandy- and sedative-blurred perception; her sightings of Forrest may be hallucination, conscience, or haunting, and she withholds her 'dark secret' even from herself.
unreliable_frame.quote: even their wildest speculations were not bold enough to guess her dark secret

setting_as_constraint.value: The big isolated hill house at Burlingame, emptied of the social swarm after Forrest's death, with only the servant Annie present and often off duty, leaves Janet alone with the apparitions; the narrow three-lane highway traps her so she cannot stop when the moths swarm.
setting_as_constraint.quote: It was Annie’s day off and she was alone in the big house.

evidence_type.value: Physical/documentary token — the heavy baroque key to the town apartment that Forrest bought from her lover, exposing the affairs; echoed by the white moth found clenched in the drowned Janet's fist.
evidence_type.quote: Forrest had reached in his pocket and drawn out a heavy, baroque key

false_suspect.value: No formal investigation occurs; the nearest suspicion falls on Janet herself for Forrest's sudden death, and briefly on the opportunistic young stranger Jack Loren, though neither is shown to have killed anyone.
false_suspect.quote: “Jack says he can use that hundred dollars. I’ll personally vouch for him”

technical_detail.value: The folk belief Forrest taught Annie — that a white moth is a wandering lost soul never to be killed — supplies the mechanism of the haunting and of Janet's fatal lunge into the pool.
technical_detail.quote: never to kill a white moth because it was a wandering soul searching for peace

moral_ambiguity.value: Forrest, the wronged husband, lures rather than harms; and Janet is given a genuine grievance — decades married to an old man, wanting 'something out of life' — so her betrayal is comprehensible rather than simply wicked.
moral_ambiguity.quote: “don’t I deserve something out of life before I’m too old to care?”
